papers.title: Thermostable Carbohydrate-Active Enzymes for High-Temperature Biomass Conversion: From Molecular Design to Process Integration.
papers.abstract: High-temperature processing of carbohydrate-rich biomass, including starch liquefaction and lignocellulose saccharification, can improve sugar yields, reduce contamination risks, and facilitate integration with thermochemical pretreatments. However, the operational stability of native carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) at 60-90 °C remains a major bottleneck for efficient and economically viable biorefineries, and existing reviews rarely integrate multiscale molecular mechanisms with process-relevant engineering strategies. This review systematically examines the multiscale basis of thermost
papers.summary: This review examines the molecular and structural basis of thermostability in carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) and how these mechanisms can be leveraged for high-temperature biomass conversion processes such as starch liquefaction and lignocellulose saccharification. It connects protein-level design strategies—including rational design, directed evolution, and computational approaches—with process-level integration for biorefineries operating at 60–90 °C. The work aims to bridge the gap between mechanistic understanding and practical engineering of thermostable enzyme systems.

papers.title: Persistent Local Laplacian Prediction of Protein-Ligand Binding Affinities.
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of protein-ligand binding affinity remains a central challenge in structure-based drug discovery. The effectiveness of machine learning models critically depends on the quality of molecular representations, for which advanced mathematical frameworks provide powerful tools. In this work, we employ a novel mathematical theory, termed the persistent local Laplacian (PLL), to construct molecular descriptors that capture localized geometric and topological features of biomolecular structures. The PLL framework addresses key limitations of traditional topological data analysis me
papers.journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
papers.summary: The paper introduces a new mathematical framework called persistent local Laplacian (PLL) to build molecular descriptors that capture local geometric and topological features of protein-ligand complexes. These descriptors are used to train machine learning models for predicting binding affinity, aiming to improve on traditional topological data analysis methods. The approach addresses limitations in how molecular representations encode localized structural information for drug discovery.

papers.title: Structure-Based Engineering for PTPσ-Targeted Therapeutic Development.
papers.abstract: Protein tyrosine phosphatase sigma (PTPσ) is a member of the leukocyte common antigen-related (LAR) family of receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatases. Its architecture integrates an extracellular proteoglycan-sensing region, a single-pass transmembrane helix, and tandem intracellular phosphatase domains. In neural injury, inhibition of PTPσ signaling can relieve chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan (CSPG)-mediated restriction of axonal growth and plasticity. In rheumatoid arthritis (RA), by contrast, restoration of PTPσ activity in fibroblast-like synoviocytes can suppress pathogenic migration
papers.summary: This review discusses structure-based engineering strategies for developing therapeutics targeting PTPσ, a receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatase involved in neural injury and rheumatoid arthritis. The authors highlight how PTPσ's multi-domain architecture—extracellular proteoglycan-sensing region, transmembrane helix, and tandem intracellular phosphatase domains—can be exploited for drug design. The key insight is that PTPσ modulation has context-dependent therapeutic goals: inhibiting it to promote axonal growth after neural injury versus restoring its activity to suppress pathogenic synoviocyte migration in rheumatoid arthritis.

papers.title: Unique features of EIGHT fold-Proteins with the most complex 83 knotted topology.
papers.abstract: Herein, we present three crystal structures of the most complex knotted protein to date, an [Formula: see text] knot with eight crossings, which belongs to a clasp knot family. The fold of this protein is also unique, and we call it the EIGHT fold (Extraordinarily Intricate Globular Helical Tangled fold). The [Formula: see text] knot is found only in a certain group of bacteria, where it is strictly conserved, despite sequence identities as low as 10%. The [Formula: see text] structure shows a high level of internal symmetry, with structurally analogous halves. It is possible that the EIGHT fo
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
papers.summary: This paper reports the first crystal structures of a protein with an 8-crossing knot (8₂₁), the most complex protein knot known to date, found in a specific group of bacteria and strictly conserved despite low sequence identity. The authors define a new fold, the EIGHT fold, which shows internal structural symmetry between halves, suggesting a possible duplication or folding pathway. These structures expand the known limits of protein knot complexity and provide a basis for understanding how such intricate topologies fold and evolve.

papers.title: Oleanolic acid-hesperetin co-assembled nanoparticles alleviate neurological injury after ischemic stroke via the PI3K/AKT/GSK-3β axis.
papers.abstract: Ischemic stroke remains a leading cause of death and long-term disability, while the current clinically applicable adjunctive neuroprotective strategies face substantial limitations. Oleanolic acid and hesperetin exhibit synergistic antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-apoptotic activities; however, their poor aqueous solubility and limited bioavailability remain major limitations to their therapeutic development. Oleanolic acid and hesperetin were formulated as co-assembled nanoparticles using an emulsion-solvent evaporation method. A 5:2 mass ratio of oleanolic acid to hesperetin produce
papers.summary: This study formulates oleanolic acid and hesperetin into co-assembled nanoparticles to overcome their poor solubility and bioavailability, and tests them in a model of ischemic stroke. The nanoparticles alleviate neurological injury, with the authors attributing the protective effect to modulation of the PI3K/AKT/GSK-3β signaling axis.

papers.title: Innovative design and development of novel thiazole-paracetamol hybrids as COX inhibitors and immunomodulatory activity: design, synthesis, SAR, in vitro biological evaluation, and molecular docking analysis.
papers.abstract: The hybridization approach was employed to design a single pharmacophore based on the conjugation of paracetamol with thiazole derivatives, yielding thiazole-paracetamol hybrid derivatives 4-11 that utilize a linker from hydrazone (-C[double bond, length as m-dash]N-NH) and azo (-N[double bond, length as m-dash]N-) linkers, serving as the hydrogen bond donor/acceptor binding site. The structure of the designed derivatives was fully characterized and confirmed using analytical data (IR, 1H NMR, and 13C NMR), and elemental analysis. The anti-inflammatory potential of the synthesized hybrids was
papers.summary: This study designs and synthesizes a series of hybrid molecules combining paracetamol with thiazole derivatives via hydrazone or azo linkers, aiming to create dual-acting COX inhibitors with immunomodulatory properties. The compounds were characterized spectroscopically and evaluated in vitro for anti-inflammatory activity, with structure-activity relationships and molecular docking supporting their binding to COX enzymes. The work represents a medicinal chemistry effort to repurpose a common analgesic scaffold into more potent anti-inflammatory agents.

papers.title: RAF isoform selectivity of MEK inhibitors and rational design of a covalent ARAF-MEK inhibitor.
papers.abstract: Aberrant activation of the RAS/RAF/mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MEK)/extracellular signal-regulated kinase pathway is a frequent cause of cancer. Allosteric MEK inhibitors block this pathway by binding RAF-MEK complexes to prevent activation of MEK by RAF. However, how MEK inhibitor potency varies across the three RAF isoforms remains poorly understood. We profiled seven allosteric MEK inhibitors and observed a notable hierarchy of sensitivity: All most potently inhibited CRAF-driven MEK activation while relatively sparing ARAF-driven activation. We identified point mutations in AR
papers.summary: This study profiles seven allosteric MEK inhibitors and finds a consistent potency hierarchy across RAF isoforms: they most strongly block CRAF-driven MEK activation and relatively spare ARAF-driven activation. Using point mutations in ARAF to map the structural basis of this selectivity, the authors rationally design a covalent ARAF-MEK inhibitor that overcomes the ARAF-sparing limitation.

papers.title: A recyclable [DABCO][Imi]2 deep eutectic solvent for multicomponent synthesis of 1,2-dihydropyridine-3-carbonitriles: in vitro antiproliferative and in silico molecular evaluation.
papers.abstract: This study reports the synthesis of a novel deep eutectic solvent (DES), [DABCO][Imi]2, for the multicomponent synthesis of 2-oxo-4,6-disubstituted-1,2-dihydropyridine-3-carbonitrile derivatives. A novel DES was successfully synthesized and structurally characterized using 1H NMR, 13C NMR, FT-IR spectroscopy, and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). A series of 30 derivatives was synthesized in moderate isolated yields (up to 40%). The synthesized compounds were evaluated for their inhibitory activity against human melanoma A375 cancer cells. Among the synthesized compounds, (5cg) and (5ch) exhib
papers.summary: The authors developed a new deep eutectic solvent, [DABCO][Imi]2, and used it as a recyclable reaction medium for multicomponent synthesis of 1,2-dihydropyridine-3-carbonitrile derivatives. Thirty compounds were made in moderate yields (up to 40%) and screened against human melanoma A375 cells, with two derivatives (5cg and 5ch) showing the most promising antiproliferative activity, supported by in silico molecular evaluation.

papers.title: Competing Isomerization Channels and Rotor Selectivity in a Third-Generation Molecular Motor: Insights from Nonadiabatic Dynamics.
papers.abstract: Third-generation light-driven molecular motors, characterized by a unique double-rotor architecture, represent a pivotal advancement in nanotechnology. Recently, a novel third-generation molecular motor based on bridged-isoindigo has been proposed. However, the microscopic mechanism behind its ultrafast photoisomerization remains to be explored. In this work, nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulations at the semiempirical OM2/MRCI level were employed to investigate the excited-state dynamics of a third-generation molecular motor, starting from the E S Z S configuration. The simulation reveals
papers.summary: This study uses nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the ultrafast photoisomerization mechanism of a third-generation light-driven molecular motor based on bridged-isoindigo. The simulations reveal competing isomerization channels and rotor selectivity starting from the E S Z S configuration, providing microscopic insight into how the double-rotor architecture governs excited-state dynamics. The work advances understanding of design principles for next-generation molecular motors in nanotechnology.

papers.title: Antibacterial Activity of Equisetin from Endophytic Fusarium incarnatum JMB4 Associated with Jatropha multifida L. Against MRSA: Experimental and In Silico Insights.
papers.abstract: An antibacterial metabolite was isolated from the endophytic fungus Fusarium incarnatum JMB4 associated with Jatropha multifida L. by bioactivity-guided chromatography and recrystallization. The isolated compound was assigned as equisetin using UV-vis, FTIR, LC-MS/MS, and 1H NMR data. Anti-MRSA activity was evaluated by disk diffusion, with chloramphenicol and amoxicillin as antibiotic comparators. At 1% (w/v; 100 μg/disk), equisetin produced an inhibition zone of 23.94 ± 0.66 mm; the recorded comparator zones were 24.71 ± 0.68 mm for chloramphenicol (30 μg/disk) and 11.76 ± 0.66 mm for amoxic
papers.summary: Researchers isolated equisetin, an antibacterial compound, from an endophytic fungus (Fusarium incarnatum JMB4) living inside the medicinal plant Jatropha multifida. Equisetin showed strong activity against MRSA in disk-diffusion assays, producing an inhibition zone comparable to chloramphenicol and much larger than amoxicillin. The study combines experimental isolation/characterization with in silico analyses to support its anti-MRSA potential.

papers.title: Effects of Coal Rank on the Adsorption Characteristics and Mechanism of Hydrogen Sulfide by Coal Molecules.
papers.abstract: This study systematically investigates the molecular structural characteristics of different rank coals (anthracite, bituminous, lignite) and their adsorption properties and mechanisms toward hydrogen sulfide (H2S). By combining X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and solid-state 13C NMR spectroscopy, it was found that aromatic carbon content increases remarkably from 55.91 to 91.75% with coal rank increasing, whereas aliphatic carbon and oxygen-bearing functional groups decrease accordingly. Macromolecular model representatives corresponding to each coal rank were constructed based on expe
papers.summary: The study characterizes how coal rank (lignite, bituminous, anthracite) affects H2S adsorption, using XPS and solid-state 13C NMR to show that aromatic carbon content rises from ~56% to ~92% with increasing rank while aliphatic and oxygen-containing groups decline. Macromolecular models were built for each rank to explain the adsorption mechanisms. The work links coal molecular structure to gas adsorption behavior relevant to coalbed methane and mine safety.

papers.title: Machine Learning in Amyloidogenic Polypeptide Research: From Sequence Prediction to Drug Discovery.
papers.abstract: Over the past decade, machine learning (ML) has established a transformative paradigm for investigating amyloidogenic polypeptides. Characterized by their propensity to form ordered, β-sheet-rich fibrillar aggregates, these polypeptides are centrally implicated in the pathogenesis of numerous neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD). This review systematically evaluates the application of ML across critical domains of amyloid investigation: sequence-based amyloidogenicity prediction, structural biology, inhibitor design, and amyloid-related cl
papers.summary: This review surveys how machine learning is being applied across amyloid research, from predicting which protein sequences are likely to form amyloid fibrils to modeling their structures and designing inhibitor drugs. It highlights ML as a unifying framework connecting sequence prediction, structural biology, and therapeutic development for neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's.

papers.title: Three Distinct Binding Modes Govern High-Affinity Ligand Interactions with Amyloid Fibrils.
papers.abstract: Fibrillar protein aggregates are a defining feature of neurodegenerative diseases and represent attractive biomarkers and therapeutic targets. However, the rational design of small-molecule ligands and probes targeting these aggregates is limited by a poor understanding of how ligands bind to amyloid fibrils. This work outlines an experimental approach to determine the binding mode of ligands to amyloid fibrils using previously overlooked information contained within standard binding assays. Using a mathematical framework to analyze binding behavior, three distinct high-affinity binding modes
papers.summary: This paper identifies three distinct high-affinity binding modes by which small-molecule ligands interact with amyloid fibrils, using a mathematical framework applied to standard binding assay data. The approach extracts previously overlooked information from routine assays to classify ligand binding behavior, which could improve rational design of amyloid-targeting probes and therapeutics.

papers.title: Mapping Ligand-Induced Conformational Changes during the Enzymatic Cycle of Human Geranylgeranyl Diphosphate Synthase.
papers.abstract: Geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthase (GGDPS) catalyzes the condensation reaction between two isoprenoid substrates: farnesyl diphosphate (FDP) and isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP), to form geranylgeranyl diphosphate (GGDP). Due to the flexible nature of the GGDPS active site and its capacity to bind multiple ligands during the reaction coordinate, understanding the structural changes that enable it to accommodate different ligands and catalyze the reaction is essential. While structures exist of substrate and product-bound GGDPS, a lack of high-resolution apo or Mg2+-only structures prevents com
papers.summary: This study maps the conformational changes in human geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthase (GGDPS) as it binds substrates and cofactors during its catalytic cycle. By obtaining high-resolution structures of the apo and Mg2+-bound states, the authors reveal how the flexible active site rearranges to accommodate different ligands. These findings fill a gap in understanding the enzyme's mechanism and could inform drug design targeting GGDPS.

papers.title: Substrate-bound structures of yeast ALA synthase reveal protein dynamics initiating heme biosynthesis.
papers.abstract: Heme is an essential prosthetic group involved in multiple biological processes in nearly all organisms. Heme biosynthesis is initiated by the pyridoxal 5'-phosphate-dependent enzyme aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS). Mutations in ALAS cause multiple hematological diseases. Despite sharing approximately 70% sequence similarity, ALAS homologs exhibit distinct expression and regulatory mechanisms. However, the molecular basis for their functional divergence remains poorly understood. Here, we used x-ray crystallography and molecular dynamics simulations to elucidate the structure and dynamics
papers.summary: This study reports substrate-bound crystal structures of yeast aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS), the enzyme that catalyzes the first step of heme biosynthesis, combined with molecular dynamics simulations. The structures reveal protein dynamics that initiate heme biosynthesis and help explain how ALAS homologs with ~70% sequence similarity diverge functionally despite their similarity. These insights are relevant to understanding hematological diseases caused by ALAS mutations.

papers.title: Harnessing the ubiquitin-proteasome system: advances and challenges of PROTACs in breast cancer.
papers.abstract: Breast cancer is one of the most significant health issues in the world, and resistance to treatment and a lack of targets that can be addressed with drugs limit the effectiveness of the existing treatment options. The development of proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) has shifted the concept of occupancy-based inhibition toward event-based targeted protein degradation. Avoiding ubiquitin-proteasome hijacking, PROTACs target disease-relevant proteins to E3 ligases, allowing them to be catalytically degraded, thereby eliminating formerly undruggable or resistant targets. Their modular desi
papers.summary: This review examines proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) as an emerging therapeutic strategy for breast cancer, shifting from occupancy-based inhibition to event-based targeted protein degradation. PROTACs recruit disease-relevant proteins to E3 ligases for catalytic degradation, potentially overcoming treatment resistance and addressing previously undruggable targets. The authors discuss advances and remaining challenges in applying this modular technology to breast cancer.

papers.title: Phospholipase Fluorogenic Probes and Molecular Determinants of Cyclic Guanosine Monophosphate-Adenosine Monophosphate Binding to Cyclic Oligonucleotide-Based Antiphage Signaling System CapV.
papers.abstract: Cyclic oligonucleotide-based antiphage signaling systems (CBASS) protect bacteria from bacteriophage infection by producing cyclic nucleotide second messengers that activate downstream effector proteins. Cyclic guanosine monophosphate-adenosine monophosphate (cGAMP)-activated phospholipase in Vibrio (CapV) is a prevalent CBASS effector whose activity is commonly monitored using the commercially available fluorogenic substrate resorufin butyrate; however, this probe is hydrolyzed by both basal and activated CapV, limiting its usefulness in CapV-related studies. Here, we report the rational desi
papers.summary: This paper describes the rational design of improved fluorogenic probes for measuring the phospholipase activity of CapV, a bacterial CBASS effector protein that is activated by the second messenger cGAMP. The authors also identify molecular determinants governing cGAMP binding to CapV. The new probes help distinguish basal from activated CapV activity, improving assays for studying this antiphage defense system.

papers.title: Zinc peroxide-coated gold nanorods as the therapeutic adjuvants for photothermal enhanced chemodynamic therapy and metalloimmunotherapy against tumor.
papers.abstract: Traditional tumor therapies have limited efficacy, leading to a high mortality rate. Although immunotherapy holds considerable therapeutic promise, clinical immunotherapy for solid tumors only elicits durable responses in a minority of patients. This limitation is largely attributed to the highly immunosuppressive nature of the tumor microenvironment (TME). Notably, conventional chemodynamic therapy (CDT) is hampered by endogenous hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) shortage in tumor cells, and AZP compensates this defect via in-situ H2O2 self-supplementation to amplify hydroxyl radical generation.
papers.summary: The authors developed gold nanorods coated with zinc peroxide (AZP) as a multifunctional therapeutic adjuvant for cancer treatment. The zinc peroxide coating self-supplies hydrogen peroxide within tumor cells, overcoming the key limitation of chemodynamic therapy, while the gold nanorods enable photothermal heating that further amplifies hydroxyl radical production. Together, this combination enhances chemodynamic therapy and triggers metalloimmunotherapy, potentially overcoming the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment.

papers.title: Diversification and functional expansion of archaeal T4F machineries.
papers.abstract: Archaea have several cell surface structures belonging to the type 4 filament (T4F) superfamily. All share a minimal core assembly system consisting of an ATPase, a platform protein, a filament-forming protein, and a class III signal peptidase. Here, we generated novel MacSyFinder2 models to identify and classify archaeal T4F systems. Our analysis revealed a vast diversity of archaeal T4F, with many organisms harboring one or more assembly machineries. Structure-based phylogenetic analysis showed that the variable N-terminal domain of T4F-related ATPases mirrors the subsystem clustering, indic
papers.summary: This study developed new computational models (MacSyFinder2) to systematically identify and classify type 4 filament (T4F) cell surface structures across archaea. The analysis revealed that archaeal T4F systems are far more diverse than previously appreciated, with many organisms carrying multiple distinct assembly machineries, and structure-based phylogenetics showed that the variable N-terminal domain of T4F ATPases tracks with subsystem classification. This work expands understanding of how these surface structures diversified and functionally specialized in archaea.

papers.title: Structural insights into the ligand modulation of MRGPRX4 conformational plasticity.
papers.abstract: Chronic pruritus is a debilitating condition with limited treatment options, particularly in cholestatic liver diseases, where bile acid dysregulation is a known trigger. Although Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor X4 (MRGPRX4) has recently been identified as a key mediator of bile acid-induced pruritus, the structural mechanisms underlying its inhibition remain poorly understood, hindering the development of therapeutic antagonists. Here, we report the cryo-electron microscopy structures of MRGPRX4 in three distinct states: agonist-bound state, antagonist-bound state, and apo state. Our s
papers.summary: This study presents cryo-EM structures of the itch receptor MRGPRX4 in agonist-bound, antagonist-bound, and apo states, revealing how ligand binding reshapes the receptor's conformation. These structures clarify the molecular basis of bile acid-induced chronic pruritus and provide a template for designing therapeutic antagonists. The work directly addresses a condition with few treatment options, particularly in cholestatic liver disease.

papers.title: Predicting Adsorbate-Solvent Interaction Energies in Zeolite Pores Using Convolutional Neural Networks with Attention Mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Solvent effects play a critical role in determining reaction thermodynamics and kinetics in liquid-phase heterogeneous catalysis, particularly in confined nanoporous environments such as zeolite pores. However, accurate prediction of solvation thermodynamics remains computationally prohibitive due to the need for extensive first-principles calculations on diverse solvent configurations. In this work, we present an attention-enhanced three-dimensional convolutional neural network (3D-CNN) framework to predict solvation interaction energies (ΔEint) of adsorbates in Ti-faujasite (Ti-FAU) zeolite
papers.journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
papers.summary: The authors developed an attention-enhanced 3D convolutional neural network to predict solvation interaction energies between adsorbates and solvents inside Ti-faujasite zeolite pores, a task normally requiring expensive first-principles calculations. By learning directly from 3D structural representations of the confined pore environment, the model offers a fast surrogate for solvation thermodynamics in liquid-phase heterogeneous catalysis. This could accelerate computational screening of solvents and reaction conditions in nanoporous catalysts.

papers.title: Computer-Aided Drug Design for Type 2 Diabetes-Related Enzymes: Polarizable and Nonpolarizable Simulations of Enzyme-Inhibitor Complexes.
papers.abstract: Carbohydrate-digesting enzymes, including pancreatic α-amylase and maltase-glucoamylase (MGAM), are important therapeutic targets for type 2 diabetes due to their role in regulating glucose production. In this study, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed to investigate the stability and interaction patterns of inhibitors identified through SILCS-based virtual screening. Representative ligands for the N-terminal and C-terminal domains of MGAM (NtMGAM, CtMGAM), and α-amylase were parametrized using both the nonpolarizable CHARMM and polarizable Drude force fields based on quantum me
papers.journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
papers.summary: This study uses molecular dynamics simulations with both standard (CHARMM) and polarizable (Drude) force fields to examine how inhibitor candidates bind to three carbohydrate-digesting enzymes relevant to type 2 diabetes: pancreatic α-amylase and the N- and C-terminal domains of maltase-glucoamylase. The work compares how well the two force-field approaches capture enzyme-inhibitor interactions, aiming to validate hits from SILCS-based virtual screening and inform drug design for glucose control.

papers.title: From Closed to Mighty: How GTP-Induced Allosteric Dynamics, Dimerization, and Membrane Binding Transform a Bacterial Dynamin-like Protein.
papers.abstract: Dynamins, crucial GTPases involved in membrane remodeling, play key roles in processes like endocytosis and membrane fission. While their importance is well-established, the precise dynamics of their conformational changes remain unclear. This study investigates the bacterial dynamin-like protein (BDLP) from Nostoc punctiforme, which undergoes a dramatic closed-to-open transition upon GTP binding. Using standard and enhanced all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, we map this transition, revealing a complex energetic landscape. The initial barrier arises from disruption of salt bridges formed
papers.journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
papers.summary: This study uses all-atom and enhanced molecular dynamics simulations to map how a bacterial dynamin-like protein from Nostoc punctiforme undergoes a dramatic closed-to-open conformational transition upon GTP binding. The work reveals a complex energetic landscape where the initial barrier involves disruption of salt bridges, and shows how GTP-induced allosteric dynamics, dimerization, and membrane binding together transform the protein. It provides mechanistic insight into the conformational cycle of dynamin-family GTPases that drive membrane remodeling.

papers.title: Unraveling a Case Where the NAC Approach Fails─MD and QM Modeling of Regioselective cis-Stilbene Oxide Hydrolysis by Engineered Epoxide Hydrolases.
papers.abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD)-based methods to predict the enantioselectivity or product specificity of enzymes typically use a near attack conformation (NAC) approach. The computational efficiency of this ground-state approach, taking minutes to hours, allows to in silico screen thousands of enzyme variants. During the computational design and screening of new variants of limonene epoxide hydrolase for improved stereoselectivity, it was noticed that, while this approach gave satisfactory prediction accuracy for most substrates, the enantioselectivity predictions were far less accurate for variants
papers.journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
papers.summary: This study investigates why the near attack conformation (NAC) approach, a fast computational method for predicting enzyme enantioselectivity, fails for certain engineered limonene epoxide hydrolase variants acting on cis-stilbene oxide. Using molecular dynamics and quantum mechanical modeling, the authors identify the limitations of the ground-state NAC method and clarify when it breaks down. The work provides guidance on when more expensive QM-based modeling is needed for reliable regioselectivity predictions.

papers.title: GDEE: A Structure-Based Platform for Gene Discovery and Enzyme Engineering.
papers.abstract: Enzymes are extensively utilized for catalyzing the production of value-added compounds in diverse sectors with significant economic impact. However, challenges such as poor protein expression, low catalytic activity, substrate/co-factor limitations, and toxicity of final products limit the efficiency of these biocatalysts. Protein engineering offers a solution by redesigning enzyme catalytic properties to enhance biosynthetic pathways. In this study, we present an automated platform for gene discovery and enzyme engineering, aimed at overcoming these bottlenecks. The GDEE platform finds and o
papers.journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
papers.summary: GDEE is an automated, structure-based platform that integrates gene discovery with enzyme engineering to address bottlenecks like poor expression, low activity, and substrate limitations in biocatalysis. It identifies candidate genes and guides redesign of enzyme catalytic properties to improve biosynthetic pathways. The platform aims to streamline the enzyme engineering workflow for producing value-added compounds.

papers.title: Assessing the Generalizability of Machine Learning and Physics-Based Methods with DNA-Encoded Libraries.
papers.abstract: Predicting protein-ligand binding is a central challenge in computational drug discovery, and while machine learning (ML) and cofolding methods have advanced rapidly, their ability to generalize beyond training or parametrization regimes remains insufficiently understood. DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) enable ultralarge screening of billions of molecules simultaneously, providing a useful testbed for evaluating these approaches at scale. A recent NeurIPS competition revealed that even top-performing ML models trained on DEL data failed at generalizing to out-of-distribution (OOD) chemical space.
papers.journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
papers.summary: This paper uses DNA-encoded library (DEL) screening data as a large-scale testbed to evaluate how well machine learning and physics-based/cofolding methods predict protein-ligand binding. It builds on a NeurIPS competition finding that top ML models trained on DEL data failed to generalize to out-of-distribution chemical space, and assesses the limits of current predictive approaches. The work highlights that strong in-distribution performance does not translate to reliable binding prediction for novel chemistry.

papers.title: CoTAR: Topology and Atomic State Reconstruction in Condensed Phases.
papers.abstract: Universal machine learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) enable performing condensed-phase molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with accuracy approaching that of first-principles; however, their lack of explicit molecular topology limits bond-aware analysis and reconnection to classical force fields. This study presents CoTAR, a hybrid graph neural network (GNN)-hidden Markov model (HMM) framework that reconstructs bond connectivity and order, formal charges, and unpaired electrons from atomic species and coordinates by combining learned local environments, chemical constraints, and temporal
papers.journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
papers.summary: CoTAR is a hybrid graph neural network and hidden Markov model framework that reconstructs molecular topology—bond connectivity, bond order, formal charges, and unpaired electrons—from atomic coordinates and species in condensed-phase simulations. This addresses a key limitation of universal machine learning interatomic potentials, which lack explicit topology, enabling bond-aware analysis and reconnection to classical force fields.

papers.title: STELLAR: A Fragment-Based Docking Workflow for Highly Flexible Long-Chain Biopolymers.
papers.abstract: Docking methods have improved significantly through optimization using generative approaches and systematic exploration of parameter configurations within docking software. However, docking large molecules such as peptides remains challenging, while the docking of large non-peptidic biopolymers is still insufficiently explored. Existing tools often exhibit limitations in both accuracy and computational efficiency when applied to longer peptides or other polymers. Moreover, although generative deep learning and machine learning approaches have shown promise, they still frequently lack robust ra
papers.journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
papers.summary: STELLAR introduces a fragment-based docking workflow designed for highly flexible long-chain biopolymers such as peptides and non-peptidic polymers. It addresses the accuracy and computational efficiency limitations of existing docking tools when handling large, flexible molecules, offering a systematic fragment-based alternative to generative deep learning approaches that often lack robustness.

papers.title: Protein interactions with small molecules, peptides and proteins share residue cluster classes.
papers.abstract: Macromolecular interactions with small molecules, peptides, and proteins are fundamental to cellular function. Despite intensive efforts to identify small-molecule modulators of protein-protein interactions (PPIs), successfully targeted interfaces remain rare, reinforcing the premise that binding sites across these molecular scale regimes possess distinct structural architectures. We previously demonstrated that the densest topological regions of protein structures, categorized as a collection of Residue Cluster Classes (cRCC), can effectively classify global protein folds and PPI. Here, we le
papers.summary: This study tests whether protein binding sites for small molecules, peptides, and proteins share common structural architectures by analyzing residue cluster classes (cRCC), the densest topological regions of protein structures. The authors find that these interaction types share cRCC classes, challenging the assumption that binding sites across molecular scale regimes are structurally distinct. This has implications for drug discovery targeting protein-protein interfaces.

papers.title: Catalysis tuned for metabolic sensing: dynamics and mechanism of the RNA methyltransferase METTL16.
papers.abstract: The methyltransferase-like protein 16 (METTL16) is the writer enzyme that methylates adenosine to form N6-methyladenosine (m6A) on U6 spliceosomal RNA and MAT2A mRNA. The latter encodes the enzyme responsible for the synthesis of S-adenosyl methionine (SAM). Since methylation influences the stability of MAT2A mRNA, METTL16 is the sensor of SAM in the cell. Here, we investigate the (co)substrate recognition and catalytic mechanism of METTL16 by a combination of in vitro and simulation methods. We first solved the crystal structures of METTL16 in complex with bisubstrate analogs (BAs), conjugate
papers.summary: This study investigates how the RNA methyltransferase METTL16 recognizes its substrates and catalyzes m6A formation on U6 spliceosomal RNA and MAT2A mRNA, the latter encoding the SAM-synthesizing enzyme. Using crystal structures with bisubstrate analogs combined with in vitro and simulation approaches, the authors dissect the (co)substrate recognition and catalytic mechanism underlying METTL16's role as a cellular SAM sensor.

papers.title: Enhancing the Activity of Ribokinase from Thermus sp. 2.9 Through Rational Design for the Cascade Synthesis of Modified Nucleotides and Nucleosides.
papers.abstract: The pursuit of efficient approaches for the production of promising antiviral and cytostatic pharmaceuticals is a crucial direction in medical biotechnology, especially after the COVID-19 pandemic. Modified nucleosides and nucleotides represent a highly promising class of chemicals for the development of drugs against cancer and viral infections. Being an alternative to traditional chemical synthesis, cascades of nucleic exchange enzymes offer single-step synthesis of such compounds with exceptional stereo- and regioselectivity. Furthermore, employing thermostable enzymes for such cascades off
papers.summary: The authors used rational protein design to engineer a more active ribokinase from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus sp. 2.9, aiming to improve a multi-enzyme cascade for producing modified nucleosides and nucleotides. These compounds are valuable for antiviral and anticancer drug development, and thermostable enzymes enable more robust single-step synthesis with high stereo- and regioselectivity. The work demonstrates how enzyme engineering can enhance biocatalytic routes to pharmaceutically relevant nucleoside analogs.

papers.title: Benzothiazole-Derived Compounds as Potential Drugs for the Treatment of Type 2 Diabetes: A Descriptive Review.
papers.abstract: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is a multifactorial metabolic disease in which hyperglycemia coexists with insulin resistance, β-cell dysfunction, dyslipidemia, and progressive microvascular and macrovascular complications. The structural versatility of the benzothiazole scaffold has enabled the development of a diverse array of preclinical compounds capable of modulating multiple diabetes-relevant targets. This review critically analyzes the available evidence on benzothiazole-derived compounds exhibiting antidiabetic or other diabetes-related pharmacological activities. No lower publication-date limit
papers.summary: This review surveys benzothiazole-derived compounds that show preclinical antidiabetic activity, covering their ability to modulate multiple targets relevant to type 2 diabetes such as hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, and β-cell dysfunction. It catalogs the structural versatility of the benzothiazole scaffold and the range of diabetes-related pharmacological effects reported in the literature. The paper is a descriptive synthesis of preclinical evidence rather than new experimental data.

papers.title: Conformational Sampling of CPT1A Enables Dynamic Structure-Based Ligand Screening.
papers.abstract: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1A) catalyzes a rate-limiting step in fatty acid β-oxidation and is a target for studies of metabolic disease and cancer. However, the structural dynamics of CPT1A remain poorly understood due to the lack of full-length structure. In this study, we employed an integrated computational approach combining molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, Markov state models (MSMs), and binding free energy calculations to elucidate the conformational landscape of human CPT1A. We performed an all-atom MD simulation of CPT1A embedded in a realistic outer mitochondrial membr
papers.summary: This study uses molecular dynamics simulations, Markov state models, and binding free energy calculations to map the conformational landscape of full-length CPT1A embedded in a mitochondrial membrane, a protein lacking a complete experimental structure. The work reveals distinct conformational states that could be targeted for structure-based ligand screening, offering a dynamic structural framework for drug discovery against this metabolic and cancer target.

papers.title: Rational Design and Delivery of Engineered Peptides: Toward a Unified Framework for Structure, Screening, and Application.
papers.abstract: This review presents a three-tiered engineering framework that systematically addresses these barriers. First, we survey chemical and sequence-based stabilization strategies, including lipidation, backbone N-methylation, and cyclization, that convert labile natural peptides into protease-resistant scaffolds. Second, moving beyond generic stabilization, we dissect the rational design of effector-inhibitory peptides, with particular emphasis on disulfide bond topology engineering as a powerful means to lock binding-competent conformations, alongside structure-guided interface optimization. Third
papers.summary: This review proposes a three-tiered framework for engineering therapeutic peptides, covering chemical stabilization strategies (lipidation, N-methylation, cyclization) to improve protease resistance, rational design of effector-inhibitory peptides with emphasis on disulfide topology engineering and structure-guided interface optimization, and downstream screening and delivery considerations. It aims to unify structure, screening, and application into a coherent design workflow.

papers.title: Design and Evaluation of Novel Peptides Targeting Protein Disulfide Isomerase as Antiplatelet Agents.
papers.abstract: Extracellular protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) is a critical mediator of thrombus formation and a promising target for novel antithrombotic therapies aiming to overcome the bleeding risks associated with current antiplatelet agents. This study aimed to design and evaluate novel, targeted peptide-based PDI inhibitors with a safe physiological profile. We utilized a bioinformatics-driven rational design approach, based on the evolutionary conservation of the PDI active site, to generate a library of 34 targeted peptides. The inhibitory mechanism and biological efficacy of the lead candidate, pe
papers.summary: The authors used evolutionary conservation of the PDI active site to rationally design a library of 34 peptides targeting extracellular protein disulfide isomerase, aiming for antithrombotic agents with reduced bleeding risk. A lead peptide was characterized for its inhibitory mechanism and biological efficacy. This is an early-stage drug-design study proposing peptide-based PDI inhibitors as safer antiplatelet candidates.

papers.title: Computational Prediction of the Therapeutic Mechanisms From the Turmeric-Pueraria-Coix Seed Botanical Formula in Rheumatoid Arthritis.
papers.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is characterized by progressive synovial inflammation and immune-metabolic reprogramming. The polyphenol-rich Turmeric-Pueraria-Coix seed (TPC) formula shows therapeutic potential against RA, though its multi-target mechanisms remain uncharacterized. To explore how TPC modulates ferroptosis and oxidative stress in RA, we integrated systems nutrition network analysis with multicohort transcriptomic datasets to identify candidate targets. Ensemble machine learning algorithms and independent cohort validation prioritized key biomarkers. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation
papers.summary: This study uses network analysis, machine learning, and molecular dynamics simulation to predict how a turmeric-Pueraria-Coix seed botanical formula may treat rheumatoid arthritis by modulating ferroptosis and oxidative stress. The authors identify candidate targets and prioritize biomarkers across multiple transcriptomic cohorts, though the work is computational and lacks experimental validation.

papers.title: Exploring Non-Covalent Pin1-PROTACs Insights Into Degradation Efficiency in Multiple Myeloma Cell Line.
papers.abstract: Pin1 is a peptidyl-prolyl isomerase involved in key signalling pathways and upregulated in different cancers, including Multiple Myeloma (MM), where it is linked to poor prognosis/drug resistance. Despite its therapeutic relevance, Pin1 remains challenging to target with conventional inhibitors thereby motivating interest in Targeted Protein Degradation (TPD) strategies. All reported Pin1-PROTACs rely on covalent Pin1 ligands, leaving non-covalent degraders largely unexplored. Since PROTACs (PROteolysis TArgeting Chimeras) act catalytically/reversibly, non-covalent designs are attractive. Here
papers.summary: This study explores non-covalent PROTACs targeting the Pin1 isomerase, which is upregulated in multiple myeloma and linked to poor prognosis. Unlike prior Pin1-PROTACs that rely on covalent ligands, the authors design and evaluate non-covalent degraders, assessing their degradation efficiency in a multiple myeloma cell line. The work provides initial insights into whether reversible, catalytic PROTAC designs can effectively degrade Pin1.

papers.title: Network pharmacology-driven identification of PTP1β and rational design of simufilam-based allosteric inhibitors for neuroprotection in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that predominantly affects elderly people and is characterized by cognitive decline and dementia. Protein tyrosine phosphatase-1B (PTP1B) is known to modulate pro-inflammatory mediators, and its overexpression in the brain has been implicated in AD-associated neuroinflammation. This study explores the mechanism of A20, A26, and co-crystal-designed compound targeting non-competitive allosteric PTP1B enzyme inhibition for AD therapy using network pharmacology and computational studies. Protein-protein interaction was designed f
papers.summary: This study uses network pharmacology and computational modeling to identify PTP1B as a target for Alzheimer's disease and to design simufilam-based allosteric inhibitors. The authors propose that non-competitive allosteric inhibition of PTP1B could reduce neuroinflammation and provide neuroprotection. The work is largely computational and requires experimental validation.

papers.title: Taxifolin targets HMGCR, LDLR and APOB to ameliorate hyperlipidemia: insights from systems pharmacology and nanoemulsion-based delivery.
papers.abstract: Hyperlipidemia is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, highlighting the need for safer and effective therapeutic options. This study evaluated the anti-hyperlipidemic potential of taxifolin (TXF) and its nanoemulsion formulation (TXF-NE) using integrated computational and experimental approaches. Network pharmacology identified 177 common targets between TXF and hyperlipidemia, with enrichment analyses linking these targets to lipid metabolism, cholesterol regulation, and inflammatory pathways. Protein-protein interaction analysis revealed key lipid-regulating genes, including HMGCR
papers.summary: This study uses network pharmacology to identify 177 shared targets between the flavonoid taxifolin and hyperlipidemia, highlighting HMGCR, LDLR, and APOB as key lipid-regulating nodes. The authors then formulate taxifolin into a nanoemulsion (TXF-NE) and test its anti-hyperlipidemic effects experimentally, suggesting improved delivery may enhance efficacy. The work combines computational target prediction with a formulation strategy to propose taxifolin as a safer alternative for managing high cholesterol.

papers.title: A phospholipase B effector exploits membrane lipid divergence to drive inter-Bacteroides competition and enables universal genome editing.
papers.abstract: The Type VI secretion system (T6SS) mediates interbacterial competition, yet the mechanisms underlying its effector diversity and cell-targeting specificity remain poorly understood. Here, we identify Btle, a phospholipase B (PLB) effector defining a unique Tle subfamily (Tle7), encoded in approximately 18.0% of Bacteroides fragilis strains. Lipidomic profiling reveals that Btle preferentially targets Bacteroides glycerophospholipids, disrupting membrane integrity and driving strict inter-Bacteroides competition, with self-intoxication prevented by the cognate immunity protein Btli1. Guided by
papers.summary: The authors identify Btle, a phospholipase B effector of the Type VI secretion system that defines a new Tle subfamily (Tle7) present in ~18% of Bacteroides fragilis strains. Lipidomic profiling shows Btle preferentially targets Bacteroides glycerophospholipids, driving strict inter-Bacteroides competition while a cognate immunity protein prevents self-intoxication. The work also leverages this effector system to enable universal genome editing in Bacteroides.

papers.title: Molecular dynamics analysis of T567 phosphorylation-induced conformational changes in ezrin.
papers.abstract: Ezrin, a key member of the ERM (Ezrin-Radixin-Moesin) family, links the plasma membrane to the actin cytoskeleton and is regulated by a conformational switch between closed and open states. Although phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate binding and phosphorylation at Thr567 are known to promote Ezrin activation, the associated conformational mechanism remains incompletely understood. Here, we combined Martini coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations with enhanced sampling, all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, and MM/PBSA calculations to compare wild-type Ezrin with the phosphomimetic
papers.summary: This study uses coarse-grained and all-atom molecular dynamics simulations with enhanced sampling to compare wild-type ezrin with a phosphomimetic mutant at Thr567, aiming to clarify how phosphorylation drives the conformational switch from the closed to the open, active state. The work provides mechanistic insight into the activation of ERM-family proteins that link the plasma membrane to the actin cytoskeleton.

papers.title: A single amino acid mutation alters substrate specificity towards l-glucose in a bacterial l-galactose dehydrogenase.
papers.abstract: Structure-based mutagenesis was performed to modify the substrate specificity of bacterial l-galactose dehydrogenase from Luteolibacter sp. strain LG18, which also exhibits intrinsic l-glucose dehydrogenase activity. Based on previously reported crystal structures of the enzyme in ternary complex with l-galactose or l-glucose and NADP+, an M212Q mutant was generated and found to exhibit a pronounced preference for l-glucose. Kinetic analysis showed that the M212Q mutant displayed an approximately 20-fold higher k cat/K M value for l-glucose than for l-galactose. To elucidate the structural bas
papers.summary: The authors used structure-based mutagenesis to alter the substrate specificity of a bacterial L-galactose dehydrogenase that also has intrinsic L-glucose dehydrogenase activity. A single M212Q mutation shifted the enzyme's preference strongly toward L-glucose, giving a ~20-fold higher catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) for L-glucose over L-galactose. This demonstrates that a single amino acid change can effectively reprogram sugar substrate specificity in this enzyme family.

papers.title: Rational structure-guided identification of a Bcl-2-targeting peptide with antiproliferative effects on colorectal cancer cells.
papers.abstract: Bcl-2 is critical for tumour survival and serves as a promising anticancer drug target. Herein, a series of novel Bcl-2-targeted peptides were identified through structure-based virtual screening and systematic biological validation. Four candidate peptides were selected from the peptide library. MST results demonstrated that Peptide 1 exhibited the strongest apparent binding affinity towards Bcl-2 (Kd = 0.51 ± 0.03 μM), superior to VS-9 and other screened peptides. Molecular dynamics simulation, free energy landscape analysis, and MM/GBSA calculation further supported the predicted conformati
papers.journal: Journal of enzyme inhibition and medicinal chemistry
papers.summary: The authors used structure-based virtual screening to identify peptides that bind Bcl-2, an anti-apoptotic protein that supports tumour survival, then validated the top candidates experimentally. Peptide 1 showed the strongest binding affinity (Kd ≈ 0.51 μM), and molecular dynamics and free energy calculations supported the predicted binding mode. The peptide also inhibited proliferation of colorectal cancer cells, suggesting a starting point for Bcl-2-targeting anticancer peptide development.

papers.title: Context-dependent protein structure prediction analysis and complex stoichiometry inference with MultimerMapper.
papers.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed the field of structural biology, notably with the accuracy level reached by AlphaFold in the prediction of protein structures. While cloud implementations have broadened access to these methods, there is still a lack of non-AI tools to systematically interpret and analyze the resulting data, especially under varying modeling contexts. Here, we present MultimerMapper, a pipeline and software suite designed to generate, extract, integrate, analyze, and visualize the behavior of multimeric systems in ensembles of overlapping protein struct
papers.summary: MultimerMapper is a new software pipeline that systematically generates, extracts, integrates, analyzes, and visualizes how multimeric protein complexes behave across ensembles of overlapping predicted structures, addressing a gap in non-AI tools for interpreting AlphaFold-style outputs under varying modeling contexts. It also enables inference of complex stoichiometry from these structure ensembles. The work provides a practical toolkit for downstream analysis of AI-predicted structural data.

papers.title: Multi-omics integration reveals the role of PFOS in sarcopenia via ESRRG and RBP4: from computational prediction to experimental validation.
papers.abstract: Perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) has been shown to cause multi-organ dysfunction; however, the specific mechanisms underlying its association with sarcopenia remain unclear.
papers.summary: This study integrates multi-omics data with computational prediction and experimental validation to investigate how exposure to PFOS, a persistent environmental pollutant, contributes to sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss). The authors identify ESRRG and RBP4 as key mediators of PFOS-associated muscle dysfunction, linking pollutant exposure to specific molecular pathways.

papers.title: Case Report: Liangxue Jiedu Huayu Formula as adjunctive therapy for leptospirosis with Weil's syndrome.
papers.abstract: Leptospirosis is a global zoonotic disease with over one million cases annually worldwide. Approximately 5%-10% of patients progress to Weil's syndrome, characterized by multi-organ failure and high mortality, but treatment options remain limited. This report describes a patient with severe leptospirosis who showed marked improvement following treatment with Liangxue Jiedu Huayu Formula (LXJDHYF), a traditional Chinese medicine formula, and explores potential mechanisms.
papers.summary: This case report describes a single patient with severe leptospirosis complicated by Weil's syndrome (multi-organ failure) who showed marked clinical improvement after receiving Liangxue Jiedu Huayu Formula, a traditional Chinese medicine decoction, as an adjunct to standard care. The authors also speculate on possible mechanisms of action. As a single case report, it provides only preliminary, hypothesis-generating evidence.

papers.title: Multi-source data integration and ensemble machine learning analysis of the role of Corilagin in regulating endoplasmic reticulum stress and alleviating intestinal ischemia reperfusion injury in mice.
papers.abstract: Intestinal ischemia-reperfusion injury (IIRI) is driven by oxidative stress, excessive inflammation, Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress (ERS), and disruption of the intestinal epithelial barrier. Corilagin, a natural ellagitannin with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities, has shown protective effects against IIRI; however, its cross-species and multitarget mechanisms remain unclear.
papers.summary: This study integrates multiple data sources with ensemble machine learning to investigate how the natural compound Corilagin protects against intestinal ischemia-reperfusion injury in mice, focusing on endoplasmic reticulum stress. The authors identify multi-target mechanisms and cross-species evidence linking Corilagin's antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects to ERS regulation and intestinal barrier protection.

papers.title: Exploring molecular interactions between yeast topoisomerase I and RNA polymerase III subunit, Rpc82 using an in-silico approach.
papers.abstract: The process of DNA transcription leads to the generation of torsional stress, which must be resolved for smooth progression of the transcription machinery. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, DNA topoisomerase I (Top I), a type IB topoisomerase, plays a critical role in relaxing supercoils and mitigating the topological strain associated with transcription. While several proteins from the transcription machinery have been reported to interact with yeast Top I, the precise structural domains involved and the detailed features of the interaction interfaces remain largely unexplored. This gap is partly
papers.summary: This study uses computational docking and molecular interaction analysis to model how yeast topoisomerase I (Top I) binds to Rpc82, a subunit of RNA polymerase III, in order to relieve transcription-associated torsional stress. The authors identify putative structural domains and interface features of the Top I–Rpc82 interaction, which had not been characterized experimentally. The work is purely in-silico and provides hypotheses for future experimental validation.

papers.title: In silico evaluation of potential penicillin-binding protein 2 (PBP2) inhibitors from Borassus flabellifer haustorium against cephalosporin-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
papers.abstract: The emergence of cephalosporin-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae strains, encoding altered Penicillin-Binding Protein 2 (PBP2), has become a major global public health concern. The increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance necessitates the development of novel antimicrobial agents. In the present study, phytocompounds derived from the haustorium of Borassus flabellifer L. were investigated as potential inhibitors of PBP2 using an integrated in silico approach.
papers.summary: This study uses computational docking and related in silico methods to screen phytochemicals from the palm Borassus flabellifer (palmyra palm) haustorium as potential inhibitors of penicillin-binding protein 2 (PBP2) from cephalosporin-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The work aims to identify plant-derived lead compounds that could address the growing problem of drug-resistant gonorrhea, though the findings are purely computational and require experimental validation.

papers.title: Immunoinformatics and reverse vaccinology design of self-amplifying RNA vaccine against marburg virus with structural dynamics and immune simulation analysis.
papers.abstract: Marburg virus disease (MVD), a deadly zoonotic illness in humans, is caused by the Marburg virus (MARV), a single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the Orthomarburgvirus genus of the Filoviridae family. There are currently no approved vaccines or efficient antiviral therapies for MARV, despite high morbidity and fatality rates of the virus, particularly in Africa. Recognizing its epidemic potential and its inclusion on the WHO list of blueprint priority pathogens, an immunoinformatics approach was used to design novel multi-epitope saRNA vaccine candidates (MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII) targeting th
papers.summary: The authors used immunoinformatics and reverse vaccinology to design two multi-epitope self-amplifying RNA vaccine candidates (MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII) against Marburg virus, targeting viral proteins to elicit broad immune responses. They validated the designs with structural dynamics simulations and immune simulation analyses, suggesting the candidates are stable and immunogenic in silico. This provides a computational blueprint for a MARV vaccine, though experimental validation remains to be done.

papers.title: Investigating potential molecular mechanisms linking 6PPD-quinone exposure to Intervertebral Disc Degeneration: A network toxicology, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulation study.
papers.abstract: As an emerging pollutant derived from tire rubber, 6PPD-quinone (6PPD-Q) has raised public health concerns due to widespread environmental exposure; however, its potential toxicological effects on avascular tissues such as intervertebral discs remain unclear. This study integrated network toxicology, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation to investigate the potential mechanisms linking 6PPD-Q exposure to intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD). ADMET toxicological predictions indicated high model-predicted probabilities for SR-MMP and SR-ARE activation. Through multidimensio
papers.summary: This study uses network toxicology, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations to predict how the environmental pollutant 6PPD-quinone might contribute to intervertebral disc degeneration. The authors identify potential molecular targets and pathways, suggesting that 6PPD-Q could activate stress-related responses (e.g., mitochondrial membrane potential and antioxidant response elements) in disc tissue. The findings are computational predictions that require experimental validation.

papers.title: Carbothioamide functionalized paroxetine analogues as antiparasitic agents targeting the hypoxanthine-guanine-xanthine phosphoribosyltransferase enzyme: Synthesis, characterization, biochemical, biophysical, and in silico studies.
papers.abstract: Hypoxanthine guanine xanthine phosphoribosyl transferase (HGXPRT) is one of the central enzymes of purine salvage pathway of protozoan parasites, including Plasmodium. These parasites are purine auxotrophs, and rely on purine salvage pathway for nucleic acid synthesis. Inhibiting the enzymatic activity can effectively reduce the parasite- induced infections, including malaria. In this context, a library of new carbothioamide derivatives 1-17 of paroxetine was synthesized via single-step chemical transformation strategy with a series of substituted phenyl isothiocyanates. All compounds were pur
papers.summary: The authors synthesized a library of carbothioamide-functionalized paroxetine analogues and tested them as inhibitors of the parasite purine salvage enzyme HGXPRT, a promising antiparasitic target given that Plasmodium and related protozoa are purine auxotrophs. The study combines chemical synthesis, biochemical enzyme assays, biophysical binding studies, and in silico docking to characterize the compounds. This represents an early-stage medicinal chemistry effort to repurpose a known drug scaffold toward antimalarial/antiparasitic leads.

papers.title: Integrated analyses identify MAN1B1 as a candidate regulator of chemotherapeutic tolerance and immunosuppression in bladder cancer.
papers.abstract: Gemcitabine (GEM) resistance limits treatment efficacy in bladder cancer (BC). This study identified MAN1B1 as a key driving factor for chemotherapy resistance and malignant progression in BC.
papers.summary: This study identifies MAN1B1 as a key driver of gemcitabine resistance and malignant progression in bladder cancer. Integrated analyses further link MAN1B1 to immunosuppression, suggesting it may serve as a candidate regulator connecting chemotherapeutic tolerance with immune evasion.

papers.title: Tailoring plant-based food emulsions with oil bodies and proteins recovered by alkali aqueous extraction from rapeseed (Brassica napus L.) oilseeds.
papers.abstract: Oil bodies (OBs) and storage proteins recovered from oilseeds by aqueous extraction are promising ingredients for the development of plant-based food emulsions. This study aimed to co-extract natural OBs and storage proteins from rapeseed oilseeds, to explore the microstructure, to analyse the composition, to investigate the emulsifying properties of the proteins and to determine the impact of pH on the physical stability of natural OBs, homogenized OBs, proteins and protein-stabilized oil droplets in emulsions. Alkali aqueous extraction at pH 9.5 enabled the recovery of well-dispersed OBs tog
papers.summary: This study demonstrates that oil bodies and storage proteins can be co-extracted from rapeseed using alkaline aqueous extraction at pH 9.5, yielding well-dispersed oil bodies suitable for plant-based emulsion formulations. The authors characterized the microstructure and composition of the recovered fractions and examined how pH affects the physical stability of natural oil bodies, homogenized oil bodies, and protein-stabilized oil droplets in emulsions.

papers.title: Sequence-activity mapping and model-guided engineering of the phenol-responsive DmpR-Po σ54 promoter.
papers.abstract: Promoters are core cis-regulatory elements that determine gene expression levels and dynamic responses, and their quantitative engineering directly dictates the performance of synthetic biological systems such as whole-cell biosensors. However, the transcriptional output of complex inducible systems, exemplified by σ54-dependent promoters, relies on long-range coordination among distal bacterial enhancer-binding proteins, DNA architectural proteins, and RNA polymerase. The combined effects of multiple regulatory regions on promoter output remain poorly understood, which limits the cross-backgr
papers.summary: The authors systematically mapped how sequence variation across the regulatory regions of the phenol-responsive DmpR-Po σ54 promoter affects transcriptional output, then used the resulting sequence-activity data to build a model that guided engineering of improved promoter variants. This work clarifies how distal enhancer-binding protein sites, DNA architectural elements, and core promoter regions jointly shape expression in a complex σ54-dependent system, and demonstrates model-guided design of tunable biosensor components.

papers.title: Engineering a hemoglobin variant with enhanced stability and oxygen affinity using a protein language model.
papers.abstract: Engineered hemoglobin variants offer therapeutic promise for artificial blood substitutes and oxygen therapeutics, but rational design is constrained by protein stability and heme-binding. Protein language models (pLMs) predict mutation fitness, yet their integration with biophysical validation remains limited.
papers.summary: The authors use a protein language model to design hemoglobin variants with improved stability and oxygen affinity, then validate the designs biophysically. This demonstrates that pLM-guided mutation prediction can be combined with experimental characterization to engineer oxygen-carrying proteins, a step toward artificial blood substitutes.

papers.title: Advances and applications of engineered protein therapeutics and their role in precision medicine.
papers.abstract: Proteins are a vital class of biomolecules. They play essential roles in biological processes, including building cellular structures, forming cellular channels and receptors, catalyzing biological reactions, transporting molecules, and contributing to immune defense mechanisms. Advances in protein engineering have enabled the genetic modification of naturally occurring proteins, using recombinant deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) technology, leading to the development of therapeutic proteins with enhanced specificity, stability, and clinical performance. Despite the rapid growth of engineered biolo
papers.summary: This review surveys how protein engineering, powered by recombinant DNA technology, has produced therapeutic proteins with improved specificity, stability, and clinical performance. It discusses the expanding applications of these engineered biologics and their growing role in precision medicine, while noting challenges that remain in the field.

papers.title: Targeting Muscle-Specific E3 Ligases in Cancer Cachexia Through Structure-Based Virtual Screening of Small-Molecule Inhibitors.
papers.abstract: Cachexia is a multifactorial metabolic syndrome characterized by severe skeletal muscle loss that cannot be reversed by nutritional support. Common in cancer and other chronic diseases, it significantly increases morbidity and mortality. Muscle wasting is primarily driven by activation of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway through the E3 ubiquitin ligases MuRF1 and Atrogin-1, which promote protein degradation and muscle atrophy. This study used computational modeling and docking to identify small-molecule inhibitors targeting these ligases, including repurposed drugs with anti-cachectic potentia
papers.summary: This study uses computational modeling and molecular docking to screen for small-molecule inhibitors targeting the muscle-specific E3 ubiquitin ligases MuRF1 and Atrogin-1, which drive protein degradation in cancer cachexia. The authors identify candidate compounds, including repurposed drugs, with potential anti-cachectic activity. The work is purely computational and provides starting points for experimental validation rather than demonstrated efficacy.
